title: Plotinus and Neoplatonism
subtitle: The flight of the alone to the alone
objectives: By the end you will be able to describe Plotinus' life and how his writings, the Enneads, came to us through his student Porphyry.
By the end you will be able to explain the three levels of reality in Plotinus: the One, Intellect and Soul, and the idea of emanation that links them.
By the end you will be able to describe the 'ascent' of the soul and why Plotinus treats philosophy as a path to inner transformation.
By the end you will be able to trace how Neoplatonism shaped Christian, Islamic and Jewish thought in the centuries that followed.
hook:
Imagine a philosopher who seemed embarrassed to have a body. He would not say who his parents were or where he was born. He refused to sit for a portrait, asking why anyone would want an image of an image. He wrote with poor eyesight, never reread his own work, and yet his students believed that, a handful of times in his life, he had touched the source of all reality directly.

This is how his student Porphyry describes Plotinus in the opening lines of his *Life of Plotinus*, written around 301 CE. Plotinus lived in the third century, in a Roman Empire wracked by plagues, invasions and a rapid turnover of emperors. Yet his writing is calm, luminous and strangely intimate. He asked a question that every school we have met since Day 23 had circled in its own way: what is the deepest source of a good life? His answer was bold. The good life is a journey home, back to the One from which everything flows.

sections.heading: A Philosopher in a Troubled Empire
sections.body:
Plotinus was born around 204 or 205 CE, almost certainly in Roman Egypt. A later writer names the town of Lycopolis, but Porphyry tells us Plotinus himself never discussed his origins, so we cannot be sure. At about the age of twenty-eight he went looking for a teacher in Alexandria, the great intellectual city of the Mediterranean. He was disappointed by every lecturer he heard until a friend took him to Ammonius Saccas, an enigmatic Platonist who wrote nothing. According to Porphyry, Plotinus said: this is the man I was looking for. He stayed with Ammonius for about eleven years.

His curiosity then took him somewhere surprising. In 242–243 he joined the Roman emperor Gordian III's military campaign against Persia, hoping to learn the philosophy of the Persians and Indians. The campaign collapsed when Gordian died, and Plotinus escaped with difficulty to Antioch. At around forty he settled in Rome, where he taught for the rest of his life.

His school was informal and international. Senators, doctors, a poet, women who were serious students of philosophy, and the emperor Gallienus and his wife all appear in Porphyry's account. Plotinus even hoped to found a city of philosophers in Campania, to be called Platonopolis and run on Plato's laws; the plan came to nothing. He became ill in his final years and died in 270 in Campania. Porphyry, who was away in Sicily at the time, reports that his last words were roughly: try to bring back the god in you to the divine in the All.

Plotinus began writing only around age fifty. After his death Porphyry edited the fifty-four treatises into six groups of nine. Because the Greek for nine is *ennea*, the collection is called the **Enneads**. The arrangement is Porphyry's, not Plotinus', moving roughly from ethics up to the highest metaphysics.

sections.heading: Not 'Neo', Just Plato: Where This Philosophy Comes From
sections.body:
Today we call Plotinus the founder of **Neoplatonism**, but that label was invented by historians in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Plotinus would have been puzzled by it. He saw himself as an interpreter of Plato, explaining what the master had really meant. He insisted that his views were not new.

Still, his synthesis was original. Remember Plato's Theory of Forms from Day 11, and the Form of the Good in the Cave allegory on Day 12? In the *Republic* Plato says, almost in passing, that the Good is 'beyond being', surpassing even the Forms in dignity and power. Plotinus took that hint and built an entire universe on it. He also absorbed Aristotle (Day 18): Aristotle's unmoved mover is a mind thinking itself, and Plotinus made a self-thinking Intellect the second level of reality. From the Stoics (Day 25) he took the idea of a cosmos that is a single living, interconnected whole. And from Pythagoras (Day 3) came a fascination with unity and number.

Plotinus also argued against people. He wrote a fierce treatise against certain **Gnostics**, religious thinkers who taught that the visible world was the botched work of an ignorant or evil creator and that the elect should despise it. Plotinus thought this was both bad philosophy and bad manners toward the cosmos. The world is an image of something higher, he said, and an image of beauty is still beautiful. This is a subtle point: Plotinus wanted to rise above the physical world, but not to hate it.

sections.heading: The One: Beyond Everything We Can Say
sections.body:
At the summit of Plotinus' system stands the **One**, which he also calls the Good. Why start there? His reasoning runs like this. Everything that exists is a unity of some kind: an army, a choir, a plant, a body. Take away its unity and it stops being what it is; a scattered army is no longer an army. So unity seems to come before being. Every unity we meet, however, is also a multiplicity: a body has parts, a mind has many thoughts. So behind all these partial unities there must be something that is simply one, with no parts and no divisions at all.

This leads to a startling conclusion. If the One is absolutely simple, we cannot really describe it. To say 'the One is wise' or 'the One is a being' would add a second thing to it, splitting it into subject and quality. So Plotinus says the One is beyond being, beyond thought, even beyond the name 'One'. That name is just the best pointer we have, a way of denying all multiplicity. Our language, he admits, circles around the One from the outside.

This way of speaking about the highest reality by saying what it is *not* is called **negative theology** (also known as the apophatic way). Keep it in mind: you will meet it again in the Islamic and Jewish philosophers of Day 33, especially Maimonides, and in Christian mystics for centuries.

If the One is beyond thought, how can we know anything about it? Plotinus' answer is that we cannot know it the way we know a fact. We can only become one with it, in an experience that goes beyond reasoning. We will come back to that at the end of the lesson.

sections.heading: Emanation: How Everything Flows from the One
sections.body:
If the One is perfect and needs nothing, why does anything else exist? Plotinus does not imagine the One deciding to create, like a craftsman with a plan. That would make the One need something. Instead, he says that everything else flows from it necessarily, the way light streams from the sun or heat from fire, without the source losing anything. This process is called **emanation**. Plotinus' favorite images are a spring that feeds rivers without being drained, and the sun that shines without being diminished.

The overflow produces three main levels, which later scholars call the three **hypostases** (a Greek word meaning roughly 'underlying realities'):

1. **The One**, the source, simple and beyond being.
2. **Intellect** (*Nous*), a perfect mind that eternally thinks all the Forms. Here Plato's Forms become the thoughts of a divine mind. Intellect is where being and thinking first appear, and with them a first, gentle multiplicity.
3. **Soul**, which looks up to Intellect and down to the physical world. The World Soul animates and orders the cosmos, and our individual souls are part of this level.

Below Soul lies the physical world, and at the very bottom lies **matter**, which for Plotinus is almost nothing at all: the point where the light runs out. In one treatise he goes so far as to call matter evil itself, not because it is a wicked force but because it is a pure lack of form and goodness. That idea of evil as absence rather than a positive thing will be crucial for Augustine on Day 30.

Notice the shape of this picture. Reality is not a set of separate boxes but a great cascade of descending light. Each level contemplates the one above it and, by doing so, produces the one below. For Plotinus, even making things is a kind of contemplation spilling over. A key point is that each level is a fainter image of the one before. The further from the source, the more scattered and divided things become.

sections.heading: The Ascent: Carving Your Own Statue
sections.body:
Emanation describes a journey outward and downward. The ethical heart of Plotinus' philosophy is the journey back, the **ascent** of the soul. Plotinus held a striking view: part of our soul never fully descended. Some higher part of us remains always in contact with Intellect, even when we are completely absorbed in eating, worrying and arguing. We have forgotten it, the way you can forget a song that is still faintly playing in the background. The task of life is to turn our attention back toward it.

How? Plotinus describes stages:

- **Purification.** First comes the practice of ordinary virtues, such as self-control, courage and justice, which calm the body's pull on the soul. Then come higher, 'purifying' virtues that detach us from bodily concerns.
- **Beauty and love.** Echoing Diotima's ladder from Plato's *Symposium* (Day 15), Plotinus describes rising from beautiful bodies to beautiful actions, to beautiful souls, to the beauty of Intellect itself.
- **Philosophy and contemplation.** Dialectic, the rigorous thinking we learned from Plato, trains the mind to see the Forms.
- **Union.** Finally, beyond all thinking, comes a moment of oneness with the One.

In his treatise *On Beauty* (Ennead I.6), Plotinus offers a memorable image. If you do not yet see beauty in yourself, act like a sculptor working on a statue: cut away what is excessive, straighten what is crooked, brighten what is dull, and never stop working on your own statue until the godlike splendor of virtue shines out. Philosophy here is not information but self-sculpting.

Porphyry reports that during the six years he spent with Plotinus, his teacher reached union with the One four times. Plotinus' own descriptions are cautious. In those moments, he says, there is no seeing of an object, no 'two'; the seer and the seen are one, as two circles are one when their centers coincide. The *Enneads* close with a famous description of this life as the flight of the alone to the alone.

sections.heading: The Long Afterlife of the One
sections.body:
Plotinus' influence is enormous, though often invisible, because it usually traveled under other names.

**Later pagan Neoplatonists.** Porphyry, Iamblichus and Proclus (fifth century) developed and complicated the system. Iamblichus emphasized ritual (*theurgy*) as well as philosophy. The mathematician Hypatia of Alexandria, killed by a Christian mob in 415, taught in this broad tradition. Platonic schools continued in Athens until around 529, when the emperor Justinian restricted pagan teaching.

**Christianity.** On Day 30 you will meet Augustine, who in his *Confessions* says that reading 'books of the Platonists', almost certainly including Latin translations of Plotinus and Porphyry, freed him from thinking of God as a physical thing and helped him see evil as a lack of good. Around 500, an anonymous Christian writer known as Pseudo-Dionysius fused Neoplatonism, mostly Proclus, with Christian mysticism, and his works were treated as authoritative for a thousand years.

**Islam.** In ninth-century Baghdad, a paraphrase of parts of the *Enneads* (Books IV–VI) circulated in Arabic under the misleading title the *Theology of Aristotle*. Readers thought they were studying Aristotle's view of God. This helps explain why the great philosophers you will meet on Day 32, al-Farabi and Avicenna, built emanation schemes in which levels of intellect flow from a first, necessary being.

**Judaism and beyond.** Jewish thinkers such as Solomon ibn Gabirol in eleventh-century Spain absorbed Neoplatonic ideas, and in 1492 the Florentine Marsilio Ficino published a Latin translation of the *Enneads*, reigniting interest during the Renaissance (Day 38).

There are real objections. Critics ask whether a One 'beyond being' explains anything, or whether it is just a name for our ignorance. If the One is completely simple, why does it produce something as messy as a universe, and why exactly these levels? Others worry that Plotinus' contempt for the body, however softened, encouraged generations to treat the flesh as a prison. And philosophers since Hume (Day 49) have asked whether reports of mystical union could ever count as evidence about reality. Defenders reply that Plotinus never asked anyone to accept union on his say-so; he offered arguments first, and the experience only as a culmination of disciplined thought.

keyQuote.text: Never cease chiselling your statue, until there shall shine out on you from it the godlike splendour of virtue.
keyQuote.source: Plotinus, Enneads I.6.9 (On Beauty), trans. Stephen MacKenna

modernConnection.title: Ego Dissolution in the Laboratory
modernConnection.body:
Plotinus described moments in which the boundary between the self and the source of everything seemed to vanish. For most of the twentieth century, scientists treated such reports as outside their business. That has changed. Since the 2000s, researchers at universities such as Johns Hopkins and Imperial College London have run controlled studies in which volunteers take psilocybin, the active compound in 'magic mushrooms', or engage in long meditation retreats. Many participants describe experiences of unity, timelessness, a sense of profound meaning and difficulty putting it into words. Researchers measure these with questionnaires partly inspired by older philosophical descriptions of mysticism, such as those of William James and W. T. Stace. Neuroscientists talk about 'ego dissolution' and link it to changes in brain networks involved in self-referential thinking.

The parallels with Plotinus are striking. He too stressed that union cannot be described, that the distinction between seer and seen disappears, and that the experience changes how one lives afterward. Some study participants rank it among the most meaningful moments of their lives.

But the comparison also shows exactly where Plotinus would object. For him, union was the summit of a long ascent through virtue, beauty and rigorous thinking. A shortcut that skipped the purification would, for him, miss the point: the aim is not a peak experience but a transformed soul. Second, science can describe what happens in the brain during such experiences, but that cannot settle whether the experience reveals a deeper reality or is simply a remarkable state of the nervous system. A brain scan of someone in love does not tell you whether the beloved is worthy of love. Plotinus' claim that the One is real rests on his arguments about unity, not on the feeling alone. The modern research makes his descriptions look less exotic, but the philosophical question remains exactly where he left it.

vocabulary.definition: A modern label for the philosophy founded by Plotinus in the third century CE, which reinterpreted Plato around a single ultimate source, the One, and a hierarchy of reality flowing from it.
vocabulary.example: Neoplatonism shaped Augustine, Pseudo-Dionysius, al-Farabi and Renaissance thinkers like Ficino.

vocabulary.definition: The collected writings of Plotinus, fifty-four treatises arranged by Porphyry into six groups of nine (from Greek ennea, nine).
vocabulary.example: The famous treatise On Beauty is the sixth treatise of the first Ennead.

vocabulary.definition: For Plotinus, the absolutely simple first principle of all reality, also called the Good, which is beyond being, thought and description.
vocabulary.example: Because the One has no parts, Plotinus says even calling it 'one' is only a way of pointing.

vocabulary.definition: The process by which reality flows out of the One necessarily and without diminishing it, like light from the sun.
vocabulary.example: Through emanation, the One gives rise to Intellect, which in turn gives rise to Soul.

vocabulary.definition: A basic level of reality in Plotinus' system; the three hypostases are the One, Intellect (Nous) and Soul.
vocabulary.example: Soul is the third hypostasis, looking up to Intellect and down to the physical world.

vocabulary.definition: The second level of reality in Plotinus: a perfect divine mind that eternally thinks the Forms, so that being and thinking are united.
vocabulary.example: For Plotinus, Plato's Forms are not floating separately but are the thoughts of Nous.

vocabulary.definition: The approach of describing the highest reality by saying what it is not, because positive descriptions would wrongly limit or divide it. Also called the apophatic way.
vocabulary.example: Saying the One is not a body, not a thought and not a being is an exercise in negative theology.

vocabulary.definition: The soul's journey back toward its source through virtue, love of beauty, philosophy and finally union with the One.
vocabulary.example: Plotinus' image of carving your own statue describes one stage of the ascent: purifying the self.

thinkingExercise.title: Your Own Ladder
thinkingExercise.prompt: Plotinus thought every life is shaped by what we turn our attention toward, and that we can climb from scattered distraction toward deeper unity. Test this idea against your own experience.
steps: List three moments in your life when you felt most 'gathered together', fully absorbed and not divided against yourself. What were you doing?
List three situations in which you feel most scattered or fragmented. What pulls you apart?
Using Plotinus' sculptor image, name one thing you would 'cut away' and one thing you would 'brighten' to become more unified. Be concrete.
Ask whether Plotinus' explanation (contact with a higher reality) or a purely psychological explanation fits your 'gathered' moments better. Write a short paragraph defending your answer.
Finally, consider the strongest objection: is longing for unity a wise goal, or might a good life require embracing division, conflict and multiplicity? Write two or three sentences.

summary: Plotinus (c. 204–270 CE), who taught in Rome, founded what modern historians call Neoplatonism; his student Porphyry edited his writings as the Enneads.
At the top of reality is the One, absolutely simple and beyond being and description, so it is best approached by saying what it is not.
Everything flows from the One by emanation, like light from the sun, producing Intellect (which thinks the Forms), then Soul, then the physical world, with matter as the faintest edge.
The good life is an ascent home: purification through virtue, love of beauty, philosophy and finally union with the One, described as 'the flight of the alone to the alone'.
Through Augustine, Pseudo-Dionysius, the Arabic Theology of Aristotle and Renaissance translators, Neoplatonism deeply shaped Christian, Islamic and Jewish thought.

quiz.question: Why did Plotinus place the One above even being and thought?
options: Because the One is a physical substance like water or fire
Because any description or thought would introduce multiplicity into something absolutely simple
Because he believed the One was an evil force opposed to the Good
Because Aristotle had proved that nothing can be known
quiz.explanation: Plotinus argued that the source of all unity must itself have no parts; thinking or describing it would split it into subject and quality. It is neither physical nor evil.

quiz.question: Which image best captures Plotinus' idea of emanation?
options: A carpenter deciding to build a table from a blueprint
Two armies fighting until one wins
The sun giving off light without being diminished
A seed that must die before the plant can grow
quiz.explanation: Emanation is a necessary, effortless overflow from a source that loses nothing, like sunlight. A carpenter's deliberate plan is precisely the model Plotinus rejected.

quiz.question: What is the correct order of Plotinus' three hypostases, from highest to lowest?
options: Soul, Intellect, the One
Intellect, the One, Soul
The One, Soul, Intellect
The One, Intellect, Soul
quiz.explanation: The One comes first, then Intellect (Nous), which thinks the Forms, then Soul, which animates the physical world.

quiz.question: In Plotinus' system, where are Plato's Forms located?
options: As the thoughts of the divine Intellect
Inside physical objects, as Aristotle taught
In the One, which thinks them
Nowhere, since Plotinus rejected the Forms
quiz.explanation: Plotinus made the Forms the eternal contents of Intellect's thinking. The One is beyond thought, so it does not think them.

quiz.question: Why did Plotinus write against certain Gnostics?
options: They claimed Plato's Forms were thoughts of God
They taught that the visible cosmos was the flawed product of an ignorant or evil maker and should be despised
They denied that the soul could rise toward a higher reality
They argued that pleasure is the highest good
quiz.explanation: Plotinus thought the cosmos, though lower than Intellect, is a beautiful image of the divine. Despising it was, for him, a philosophical error.

quiz.question: Which modern situation best illustrates Plotinus' advice to 'never stop working on your own statue'?
options: Buying a sculpture as an investment
Posting edited photos to look more attractive online
Steadily breaking a habit of anger and cultivating patience over years
Memorizing a list of philosophers' names for an exam
quiz.explanation: The sculptor image is about inner self-transformation through virtue, cutting away vices and brightening the soul, not outward appearance or information.

quiz.question: How did Plotinus' ideas reach philosophers in the Islamic world?
options: Through an Arabic paraphrase of parts of the Enneads circulated as the 'Theology of Aristotle'
Through Plotinus' own travels to Baghdad
Through Ficino's Latin translation of 1492
They never reached the Islamic world
quiz.explanation: The Arabic 'Theology of Aristotle' paraphrased Enneads IV–VI under Aristotle's name, influencing al-Farabi and Avicenna. Baghdad did not yet exist in Plotinus' lifetime, and Ficino came much later.

quiz.question: Plotinus called himself a 'Neoplatonist' to distinguish his new ideas from Plato's.
quiz.explanation: The label was coined by modern historians. Plotinus presented himself as a faithful interpreter of Plato.

quiz.question: For Plotinus, matter is at the lowest edge of reality and can be called evil because it lacks form and goodness, not because it is a powerful positive force.
quiz.explanation: Plotinus treats matter as the point where the light from the One runs out, a lack rather than a rival power, an idea Augustine later developed.

quiz.question: According to Porphyry, Plotinus experienced union with the One every day of his teaching career.
quiz.explanation: Porphyry reports that Plotinus reached this union four times during the roughly six years Porphyry spent with him, which signals how rare it was.

goDeeper.body:
A lively scholarly question is whether Plotinus' system is really coherent. If the One is utterly simple and needs nothing, why does anything come from it at all? Plotinus' answer is that every perfect thing naturally produces an image of itself, as fire produces heat; generosity is built into goodness. Critics, ancient and modern, reply that this is a metaphor doing the work of an argument. Some scholars, such as Lloyd Gerson, defend Plotinus by stressing the logic of dependence: whatever is composite depends on something prior that is not composite, so an absolutely simple first principle is not a mystical extravagance but the end point of a rigorous argument about explanation. You will see a cousin of this reasoning in Avicenna's necessary being (Day 32) and in Aquinas' Five Ways (Day 35).

A second debate concerns the 'undescended soul'. Plotinus' claim that part of us always remains in Intellect was rejected by later Neoplatonists like Iamblichus and Proclus, who thought the soul descends completely and needs ritual help (theurgy) to return. This was not idle hair-splitting: it was a dispute about whether human beings can save themselves by thinking, or need outside aid. Christian debates about grace, which you will meet with Augustine, echo it.

Finally, Pierre Hadot, the French historian whose idea of 'philosophy as a way of life' frames tomorrow's review, wrote a moving short book arguing that Plotinus' metaphysics is best read as a description of inner experience and a set of spiritual exercises, not merely a theory of the universe. Whether that reading tames Plotinus too much is still argued.

readings.title: Plotinus or the Simplicity of Vision
readings.author: Pierre Hadot
readings.note: A short, beautiful introduction that reads Plotinus as a guide to inner life rather than a dry system.

readings.title: The Enneads (especially I.6 'On Beauty' and VI.9 'On the Good or the One')
readings.author: Plotinus, translated by Stephen MacKenna or in the Cambridge edition edited by Lloyd Gerson
readings.note: I.6 is the most accessible treatise; VI.9 contains the descriptions of union and the closing 'flight of the alone to the alone'.

readings.title: On the Life of Plotinus and the Order of His Books
readings.author: Porphyry
readings.note: Usually printed at the front of editions of the Enneads; a short, vivid portrait of Plotinus and his circle.

readings.title: Neoplatonism
readings.author: Pauliina Remes
readings.note: A clear survey of the whole tradition from Plotinus to Proclus.

questions: Is 'the One is beyond description' a profound insight or a way of avoiding the burden of explanation?
Can an experience that cannot be put into words count as knowledge? Why or why not?
Does Plotinus' picture of the soul's ascent encourage a healthy detachment from the body or an unhealthy disdain for it?
